title: Sql Beginner
description: Write your first query, filter and sort data with SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY and GROUP BY.

theory.contentHtml:
Lesson contents:

  • 1. Why do we need a Database?
  • 2. Database vs Excel
  • 3. Tables, rows, columns
  • 4. What is SQL?
  • Important Notes

1. Why do we need a Database?

Imagine you manage an online store. Every day there are hundreds of orders, thousands of products, and thousands of customers. If you use an Excel file, you will run into problems:

  • The file is heavy and slow to open
  • Coordinating separate local copies can be difficult
  • It is hard to link data across sheets

A Database suits structured data management and concurrent access. It stores structured data, allows fast queries, and supports many users at once.

2. Database vs Excel

+----------------+----------------------------+-------------------------------+
|    Criteria    |            Excel           |            Database           |
+----------------+----------------------------+-------------------------------+
| Capacity       | Limited to ~1 million rows | Billions of rows              |
| Search speed   | Slow with large files      | Very fast thanks to indexes   |
| Multiple users | Hard to sync               | Supported out of the box      |
| Data linking   | Use VLOOKUP                | Use JOIN (much more powerful) |
+----------------+----------------------------+-------------------------------+

3. Tables, rows, columns

A database stores data in tables. Each table consists of:

  • Column: A type of information. E.g.: full_name, salary
  • Row: A specific record. E.g.: the information of employee Alex Drew

Example table employees:

+----+--------------+-------------+----------+
| id |   full_name  |  department |  salary  |
+----+--------------+-------------+----------+
| 1  | Alex Drew    | Engineering | 12000000 |
| 2  | Brian Cooper | Marketing   | 14000000 |
+----+--------------+-------------+----------+

4. What is SQL?

SQL (Structured Query Language) is the language used to "talk" to a database. You write SQL statements to:

  • Query data: Get the list of employees
  • Filter data: Get only employees with salary > 20 million
  • Sort: Order by descending salary
  • Aggregate: Compute total salary by department

A simple SQL statement:

SELECT full_name, salary FROM employees
LIMIT 10;

The statement above gets the name and salary of at most 10 employees. Without ORDER BY, neither the selected employees nor their row order is guaranteed.

Important Notes

  • All three SQL courses use PostgreSQL in the sandbox. Keywords are case-insensitive: both SELECT and select work.
  • Unquoted identifiers fold to lowercase. "Salary" is a case-sensitive identifier; 'Salary' is a string value, not a column name. String comparison also depends on collation.
  • Each SQL statement should end with a ;
  • In this course, we will capitalize SQL keywords (SELECT, FROM, WHERE...) to make them easier to distinguish

lessons.title: The data tables in this course
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 2: The data tables in this course

theory.contentHtml:
Lesson content:

  • 1. Database diagram
  • 2. The employees table
  • 3. The products and categories tables
  • 4. The customers and orders tables

1. Database diagram

In this course, we will work with the database of a tech store made up of 5 tables:

categories (5) ──► products (20)
customers (30) ──► orders (101)
employees (30) [independent]

The arrow reads as one-to-many: one category has many products, so the products table carries a category_id column pointing back at the category; one customer has many orders, so orders carries customer_id. employees has no column pointing at another table, so it stands alone. Why the data is split this way - and how to put it back together - is the subject of the SQL Intermediate course.

2. The employees table

Stores information about the company's 30 employees:

+------------+----------------+-----------------------------------+
|   Column   |      Type      |            Description            |
+------------+----------------+-----------------------------------+
| id         | INTEGER        | Employee ID                       |
| full_name  | TEXT           | Full name                         |
| email      | TEXT           | Email (can be NULL)               |
| department | TEXT           | Engineering, Marketing, Sales, HR |
| position   | TEXT           | Manager, Team Lead, Staff         |
| salary     | NUMERIC(18, 2) | Monthly salary (VND, can be NULL) |
| hire_date  | DATE           | Format YYYY-MM-DD                 |
+------------+----------------+-----------------------------------+

3. The products and categories tables

20 tech products across 5 categories:

+------------+--------------------+
|  Category  | Number of products |
+------------+--------------------+
| Phone      | 4                  |
| Laptop     | 4                  |
| Accessory  | 6                  |
| Tablet     | 3                  |
| Smartwatch | 3                  |
+------------+--------------------+

The products table has a stock_quantity column - some products are out of stock (= 0) or not yet updated (NULL).

4. The customers and orders tables

30 customers, 101 orders from January to August 2024.

Orders have 4 statuses: Completed, Shipping, Pending, Cancelled.

Some customers have a NULL email/phone - this is the kind of real-world data you'll encounter at work.

Lesson content:

  • 1. SELECT * - Get everything
  • 2. Selecting specific columns
  • 3. Custom column order
  • 4. Limiting rows across SQL dialects
  • Important Notes

1. SELECT * - Get everything

The most basic statement in SQL:

SELECT * FROM employees
LIMIT 10;
  • SELECT = get data
  • * = all columns
  • FROM employees = from the employees table

The result returns at most 10 of the 30 rows with the 7 columns of the employees table.

2. Selecting specific columns

Instead of *, list the column names you need:

SELECT full_name, department, salary
FROM employees
LIMIT 10;

Returns only 3 columns: full name, department, and salary.

Why you should select specific columns:

  • Compact, readable results
  • Runs faster (important when the table has millions of rows)
  • Doesn't expose sensitive information (e.g. email)

3. Custom column order

You can change the column order relative to the original table:

SELECT salary, full_name FROM employees
LIMIT 10;

The salary column will be displayed before full_name.

4. Limiting rows across SQL dialects

Row-limiting syntax depends on the database. SQL Server uses TOP, while PostgreSQL uses LIMIT. This course sandbox runs PostgreSQL, so write:

SELECT full_name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC NULLS LAST, id
LIMIT 10;

DESC means descending, so larger values come first. ASC means ascending, puts smaller values first, and is the default when neither keyword is written. Here, salary DESC NULLS LAST puts higher known salaries first and missing salaries last, while id uses the default ASC order to break ties between equal salaries.

LIMIT 10 only limits the number of returned rows. ORDER BY determines which ten rows are selected and their order; without ORDER BY, SQL does not guarantee a stable “first ten” result.

Important Notes

  • SELECT * is useful for exploration; listing only needed columns reduces transferred data and avoids depending on newly added columns.
  • Simple identifiers such as salary need no quotes. Use "Inventory Value" for names with spaces; single quotes in 'salary' create a string rather than select a column.
  • Multiple columns are separated by a comma ,

Lesson content:

  • 1. WHERE - Filtering by condition
  • 2. Comparison operators
  • 3. Comparing strings
  • 4. Filtering dates
  • Important Notes

1. WHERE - Filtering by condition

Add WHERE to only get rows that meet a condition:

SELECT full_name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE department = 'Engineering'
LIMIT 10;

Returns only employees in the Engineering department.

2. Comparison operators

+----------+-----------------------+-----------------------+
| Operator |        Meaning        |        Example        |
+----------+-----------------------+-----------------------+
| =        | Equal                 | salary = 20000000     |
| != or <> | Not equal             | status != 'Cancelled' |
| >        | Greater than          | salary > 20000000     |
| >=       | Greater than or equal | salary >= 20000000    |
| <        | Less than             | price < 10000000      |
| <=       | Less than or equal    | price <= 10000000     |
+----------+-----------------------+-----------------------+

3. Comparing strings

Strings (text) must be enclosed in single quotes:

SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE status = 'Completed'
LIMIT 10;

Note: Strings are case-sensitive: 'Completed' ≠ 'completed'

4. Filtering dates

In this course's PostgreSQL sandbox, date columns such as order_date use the DATE type. PostgreSQL compares them chronologically; a half-open range is still a clear way to select a whole month:

SELECT id, order_date
FROM orders
WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01'
  AND order_date <  '2024-02-01'
LIMIT 10;

Keep dates in their standard format while filtering and calculating. Change separators or display formats only when presenting a result; converting and applying REPLACE() is not required merely to compare dates.

Important Notes

  • WHERE always comes after FROM
  • Strings use single quotes '...', not double quotes
  • Numbers do not need single quotes: salary > 20000000

lessons.title: Combining conditions with AND, OR, NOT
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 5: Combining conditions with AND, OR, NOT

theory.contentHtml:
Lesson content:

  • 1. AND - Both conditions are true
  • 2. OR - At least one condition is true
  • 3. NOT - Negation
  • 4. Combining AND and OR
  • Important Notes

1. AND - Both conditions are true

SELECT full_name, position, salary
FROM employees
WHERE department = 'Engineering' AND salary > 20000000
LIMIT 10;

Returns only employees who are both in the Engineering department and have a salary > 20 million.

2. OR - At least one condition is true

SELECT full_name, department
FROM employees
WHERE department = 'Engineering' OR department = 'Marketing'
LIMIT 10;

Returns employees in Engineering or Marketing.

3. NOT - Negation

SELECT full_name, department
FROM employees
WHERE NOT department = 'HR'
LIMIT 10;

Returns employees not in the HR department.

4. Combining AND and OR

When combining, use parentheses for clarity:

SELECT full_name, department, salary
FROM employees
WHERE (department = 'Engineering' OR department = 'Marketing')
  AND salary > 20000000
LIMIT 10;

Without parentheses, SQL evaluates NOT first, then AND, and finally OR. For example:

WHERE department = 'Engineering'
   OR department = 'Marketing' AND salary > 20000000

is interpreted as:

WHERE department = 'Engineering'
   OR (department = 'Marketing' AND salary > 20000000)

The result includes every Engineering employee, while a Marketing employee is kept only when their salary is above 20 million. To apply the salary condition to both departments, parenthesize the OR group as in the first query in this section. Explicit parentheses keep readers from having to recall precedence.

Important Notes

  • AND takes precedence over OR - always use parentheses when combining
  • You can chain multiple AND/OR: WHERE a = 1 AND b = 2 AND c = 3

NULL and three-valued logic

SQL conditions can be TRUE, FALSE, or UNKNOWN. If department is NULL, both department = 'HR' and NOT department = 'HR' are UNKNOWN, and WHERE does not keep that row. The query above therefore returns only employees whose department is known and is not HR. To keep unknown departments too, write:

WHERE department <> 'HR' OR department IS NULL

Never compare with = NULL or <> NULL; use IS NULL / IS NOT NULL.

headings.text: 2. OR - At least one condition is true

lessons.title: Advanced operators IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, IS NULL
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 6: Advanced operators IN, BETWEEN, LIKE, IS NULL

theory.contentHtml:
Lesson content:

  • 1. IN - Belongs to a list
  • 2. BETWEEN - Within a range
  • 3. LIKE - Pattern matching
  • 4. IS NULL / IS NOT NULL
  • Important Notes

1. IN - Belongs to a list

Instead of writing many ORs:

-- Verbose
SELECT full_name, department FROM employees
WHERE department = 'Engineering' OR department = 'Marketing' OR department = 'HR'
LIMIT 10;

-- More compact with IN
SELECT full_name, department FROM employees
WHERE department IN ('Engineering', 'Marketing', 'HR')
LIMIT 10;

2. BETWEEN - Within a range

SELECT product_name, price
FROM products
WHERE price BETWEEN 10000000 AND 30000000
LIMIT 10;

BETWEEN includes both ends (10 million ≤ price ≤ 30 million).

3. LIKE - Pattern matching

+-----------+------------------------------------+--------------------------------------+
| Character |               Meaning              |                Example               |
+-----------+------------------------------------+--------------------------------------+
| %         | Any string, including an empty one | '%Phone%' → contains "Phone"         |
| _         | Exactly 1 character                | '_an' → 3 characters, ending in "an" |
+-----------+------------------------------------+--------------------------------------+
SELECT full_name FROM employees
WHERE full_name LIKE 'A%'
LIMIT 10;

4. IS NULL / IS NOT NULL

NULL is a marker that no definite value is available. It is not the number 0, an empty string '', or an ordinary value. Depending on the data model, it can mean unknown, missing, or not applicable.

Because the actual value is unknown, comparing anything with NULL produces UNKNOWN rather than TRUE or FALSE:

+---------------+----------------+
|   Expression  | Logical result |
+---------------+----------------+
| email = NULL  | UNKNOWN        |
| NULL = NULL   | UNKNOWN        |
| email IS NULL | TRUE or FALSE  |
+---------------+----------------+

A WHERE clause keeps only rows for which its condition is TRUE; rows producing either FALSE or UNKNOWN are filtered out. Test for missing values with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL:

-- Employees without an email
SELECT full_name FROM employees
WHERE email IS NULL
LIMIT 10;

-- Employees who already have an email
SELECT full_name FROM employees
WHERE email IS NOT NULL
LIMIT 10;

Remember: email = NULL cannot find rows with a missing email because the comparison produces UNKNOWN, not TRUE.

Important Notes

  • IN = much more compact than many ORs
  • BETWEEN a AND b = includes both a and b
  • With the sandbox's default collation, LIKE is case-sensitive; use ILIKE for a case-insensitive search
  • Test for missing values with IS NULL / IS NOT NULL; = NULL does not produce TRUE.

lessons.title: Expressions and Aliases in SELECT
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 7: Expressions and Aliases in SELECT

theory.contentHtml:
Lesson content:

  • 1. Arithmetic expressions
  • 2. AS - Naming columns
  • 3. ROUND - Rounding numbers
  • Important Notes

1. Arithmetic expressions

You can perform calculations right inside SELECT:

SELECT product_name, price, stock_quantity,
       price * stock_quantity
FROM products
LIMIT 10;

The expression price * stock_quantity calculates inventory value. Without an alias, PostgreSQL names this result column ?column?, which does not tell the reader what it represents.

2. AS - Naming columns

Use AS to give it a nice name:

SELECT product_name,
       price * stock_quantity AS inventory_value
FROM products
LIMIT 10;

Now the column is displayed as inventory_value - neat and meaningful.

The operators you can use: +, -, *, /

3. ROUND - Rounding numbers

SELECT product_name,
       ROUND(price / 1000000.0, 1) AS price_million
FROM products
LIMIT 10;

ROUND(value, num_digits) rounds value to num_digits decimal places - for example ROUND(2490000 / 1000000.0, 1) = 2.5 (2.49 million rounded to 1 decimal place).

PostgreSQL numeric types: price is NUMERIC(18, 2), so division preserves fractional values. Use price / 1000000.0 when displaying millions; ROUND(..., 1) changes the computed value by rounding; it does not merely change its display. This two-argument form accepts NUMERIC; cast double precision to NUMERIC when specifying decimal places.

Operand types determine division: 5 / 2 returns 2 (integer division truncates toward zero), while 5 / 2.0 returns 2.5000000000000000 (NUMERIC). Casting 1.9::INTEGER rounds to 2 rather than truncating; use TRUNC(1.9) to obtain 1.

Important Notes

  • AS only changes the display name, not the underlying data
  • If the alias contains a space, use double quotes: AS "Inventory Value"
  • Division by zero raises an error in PostgreSQL; use value / NULLIF(denominator, 0) when the denominator may be zero

questions.prompt: Which statement retrieves all data from the products table?
questions.explanation: SELECT * FROM table_name is the standard syntax to get all columns. GET ALL and READ * are not valid SQL syntax.

questions.prompt: To filter employees whose salary is greater than 20 million, which statement do you use?
questions.explanation: The > operator means greater than, excluding equality. >= means greater than or equal to, and = means equal to. Aggregate FILTER does not replace WHERE for filtering rows.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct way to check for a NULL value?
questions.explanation: email = NULL produces UNKNOWN, so WHERE does not keep the row. IS NULL tests for a missing value; the string 'NULL' is ordinary text.

questions.prompt: WHERE price BETWEEN 10000000 AND 30000000 is equivalent to which statement?
questions.explanation: BETWEEN includes both bounds (inclusive), equivalent to >= AND <=. The > and < operators do not include the bounds.

questions.prompt: When combining AND and OR, which one has higher precedence?

options.label: A
options.text: OR has higher precedence than AND

options.label: B
options.text: AND has higher precedence than OR

options.label: C
options.text: Both are equal, evaluated left to right

questions.explanation: AND has higher precedence than OR. Parentheses change expression grouping; they do not promise an evaluation order or short-circuit behavior in PostgreSQL.

theory.contentHtml:
Lesson content:

  • 1. ORDER BY basics
  • 2. ASC and DESC
  • 3. Sorting by multiple columns
  • Important Notes

1. ORDER BY basics

By default, SQL does not guarantee the order of results. Use ORDER BY to sort:

SELECT full_name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary
LIMIT 10;

By default it sorts in ascending order (ASC).

2. ASC and DESC

+---------+---------------------+-------------------+
| Keyword |       Meaning       |      Example      |
+---------+---------------------+-------------------+
| ASC     | Ascending (default) | A→Z, 1→9, old→new |
| DESC    | Descending          | Z→A, 9→1, new→old |
+---------+---------------------+-------------------+
SELECT full_name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC NULLS LAST, id
LIMIT 10;

3. Sorting by multiple columns

SELECT full_name, department, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY department ASC, salary DESC NULLS LAST, id
LIMIT 10;

Sort by department A→Z, and within the same department, higher salary first.

Important Notes

  • ORDER BY comes after FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, and HAVING, but before LIMIT and OFFSET. It is therefore not always the last clause:
SELECT full_name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC NULLS LAST, id
LIMIT 10 OFFSET 0;
  • PostgreSQL sorts NULL last with ASC and first with DESC by default. Write NULLS FIRST or NULLS LAST when the position of missing values matters.
  • You can use the column number: ORDER BY 2 DESC = sort by the 2nd column

Lesson content:

  • 1. LIMIT basics
  • 2. LIMIT + ORDER BY = Top N
  • 3. OFFSET - Skip the first N rows
  • Important Notes

1. LIMIT basics

Limit the result to at most N rows:

SELECT * FROM products
LIMIT 5;

Returns at most 5 rows.

2. LIMIT + ORDER BY = Top N

This is a very common combo - getting the "Top 3 highest salaries":

SELECT full_name, salary
FROM employees
ORDER BY salary DESC NULLS LAST, id
LIMIT 3;

salary can be NULL. PostgreSQL sorts NULL first with DESC by default; NULLS LAST keeps known salaries first. id breaks ties between equal salaries.

Or the "5 cheapest products":

SELECT product_name, price
FROM products
ORDER BY price ASC, id
LIMIT 5;

3. OFFSET - Skip the first N rows

Used for pagination. A unique order such as ORDER BY id makes page boundaries deterministic, assuming the data does not change between requests:

-- Page 1: rows 1-5
SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY id LIMIT 5 OFFSET 0;

-- Page 2: rows 6-10
SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY id LIMIT 5 OFFSET 5;

Important Notes

  • LIMIT always comes after ORDER BY
  • LIMIT without ORDER BY → undefined result order
  • OFFSET counts rows to skip in the ordered result: 0 skips none, 5 skips five rows.

headings.text: 3. OFFSET - Skip the first N rows

theory.contentHtml:
Lesson content:

  • 1. The duplication problem
  • 2. DISTINCT basics
  • 3. DISTINCT with multiple columns
  • Important Notes

1. The duplication problem

When getting the list of departments:

SELECT department FROM employees
LIMIT 10;

There are 30 employees, but LIMIT 10 returns at most 10 rows; departments may repeat.

2. DISTINCT basics

Add DISTINCT to get only unique values:

SELECT DISTINCT department FROM employees
LIMIT 10;

The result has only 4 rows: Engineering, Marketing, Sales, HR.

3. DISTINCT with multiple columns

SELECT DISTINCT department, position
FROM employees
LIMIT 10;

Returns the unique pairs of department + position. For example, (Engineering, Manager) and (Engineering, Staff) are 2 different pairs.

Important Notes

  • DISTINCT goes right after SELECT
  • DISTINCT applies to the entire row, not to each column individually
  • For one column, DISTINCT collapses repeated NULL values to one row. With multiple columns it compares the whole tuple: (NULL, 'Manager') differs from (NULL, 'Staff').

questions.prompt: To get the 5 employees with the highest salaries, which statement is correct?

options.label: B
options.text: SELECT * FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC NULLS LAST, id LIMIT 5

options.label: C
options.text: SELECT * FROM employees ORDER BY salary ASC, id LIMIT 5

options.label: D
options.text: SELECT * FROM employees WHERE salary LIMIT 5

questions.explanation: ORDER BY salary DESC NULLS LAST sorts known salaries from high to low and puts NULL last; id breaks salary ties. LIMIT 5 takes at most five sorted rows. Without NULLS LAST, PostgreSQL puts NULL first with DESC.

questions.prompt: Where does DISTINCT go in a SELECT statement?

options.label: D
options.text: At the end of the query

questions.explanation: DISTINCT must go right after the SELECT keyword; it applies to the entire set of selected columns to remove fully duplicated rows. Placing it in the wrong position (after FROM/WHERE) is invalid syntax.

questions.prompt: What does ORDER BY department ASC, salary DESC NULLS LAST mean?

options.label: A
options.text: Department A→Z, salary high→low within the same department

questions.explanation: When ORDER BY has multiple columns, SQL sorts by the first column FIRST (department ASC = A→Z). For rows with the same value in the first column, it then sorts by the second column (salary DESC = high→low). NULLS LAST puts missing salaries after known salaries.

questions.prompt: With a unique ORDER BY and at least 15 rows, which rows does LIMIT 5 OFFSET 10 return?
questions.explanation: OFFSET 10 skips the first 10 rows, then LIMIT 5 takes the next 5 rows → those are rows 11 to 15. This pattern is used for pagination (page 3 with 5 rows/page).

theory.contentHtml:
Lesson content:

  • 1. COUNT(*) - Count all rows
  • 2. COUNT(column) - Count non-NULL values
  • 3. COUNT(DISTINCT column)
  • Important Notes

1. COUNT(*) - Count all rows

SELECT COUNT(*) AS total_employees
FROM employees
LIMIT 10;

Result: 30 - counts all rows, including rows with NULL.

2. COUNT(column) - Count non-NULL values

SELECT COUNT(email) AS has_email
FROM employees
LIMIT 10;

Result: 28 - only counts rows that have an email (ignoring the 2 rows where email = NULL).

3. COUNT(DISTINCT column)

SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT department) AS num_departments
FROM employees
LIMIT 10;

Result: 4 - counts the number of unique departments.

Important Notes

  • COUNT(*) counts all rows (including NULL)
  • COUNT(column) ignores NULL rows in that column
  • Always use AS to name the result column

COUNT(DISTINCT department) also ignores NULL. These queries aggregate the whole table into one row; LIMIT 10 limits output rows, not the employees being counted. On an empty table, COUNT(*) and COUNT(column) return 0.

lessons.title: Totals and averages with SUM and AVG
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 21: Totals and averages with SUM and AVG

theory.contentHtml:
Lesson content:

  • 1. SUM - Calculating a total
  • 2. AVG - Calculating an average
  • 3. Combining with WHERE
  • Important Notes

1. SUM - Calculating a total

SELECT SUM(salary) AS total_salary
FROM employees
LIMIT 10;

Calculates the total salary of all employees.

2. AVG - Calculating an average

SELECT AVG(price) AS average_price
FROM products
LIMIT 10;

Calculates the average price of all products.

Note: AVG automatically ignores NULL when calculating.

3. Combining with WHERE

SELECT SUM(total_amount) AS revenue,
       COUNT(*) AS num_orders
FROM orders
WHERE status = 'Completed'
LIMIT 10;

Calculates revenue only from completed orders.

Important Notes

  • Use SUM and AVG with numeric columns such as INTEGER, NUMERIC or REAL; the sandbox's salary column is NUMERIC(18, 2)
  • Both ignore NULL automatically
  • You can use multiple functions in a single SELECT

When there are no non-NULL input values (an empty table, no matching rows, or all-NULL values), these aggregates return NULL, not 0. Use COALESCE(..., 0) only when the business requirement calls for replacing a missing result with 0. COUNT returns 0 when there is nothing to count.

lessons.title: Smallest and largest values with MIN and MAX
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 22: Smallest and largest values with MIN and MAX

theory.contentHtml:
Lesson content:

  • 1. MIN - The smallest value
  • 2. MAX - The largest value
  • 3. The earliest date with MIN
  • 4. The latest date with MAX
  • Important Notes

1. MIN - The smallest value

SELECT MIN(price) AS lowest_price
FROM products
LIMIT 10;

2. MAX - The largest value

SELECT MAX(salary) AS highest_salary
FROM employees
LIMIT 10;

3. The earliest date with MIN

MIN and MAX also work with strings and dates. For dates, MIN is the earliest one:

SELECT MIN(hire_date) AS earliest_date
FROM employees
LIMIT 10;

4. The latest date with MAX

SELECT MAX(hire_date) AS latest_date
FROM employees
LIMIT 10;

For strings, MIN takes the first and MAX the last value according to the expression's collation. This order depends on configuration rather than always matching a human-language alphabet.

Important Notes

  • MIN and MAX work for numbers, strings, and dates
  • Both ignore NULL
  • Combine multiple functions: SELECT MIN(price), MAX(price), AVG(price) FROM products

When there are no non-NULL input values (an empty table, no matching rows, or all-NULL values), these aggregates return NULL, not 0. A COALESCE fallback must have a compatible type: COALESCE(MIN(price), 0) works for prices, whereas a fallback for MIN(hire_date) must be a date, not the number 0. Replace NULL only when the business requirement calls for it. COUNT returns 0 when there is nothing to count.

questions.prompt: How do COUNT(email) and COUNT(*) differ?

options.label: A
options.text: No difference - they give the same result

options.label: B
options.text: COUNT(email) ignores rows where email IS NULL

options.label: C
options.text: COUNT(*) only counts the first column

options.label: D
options.text: COUNT(email) counts the number of characters in the email

questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts all rows even when a column is NULL. COUNT(email) only counts rows where email is not NULL. A table of 100 rows but only 80 with an email → COUNT(*) = 100, COUNT(email) = 80.

options.label: B
options.text: Throws an error when it encounters NULL

options.label: C
options.text: Ignores rows with a NULL value

options.label: D
options.text: Returns NULL if there is any NULL

questions.explanation: AVG (like other aggregate functions such as SUM, MIN, MAX) automatically ignores NULL. AVG(salary) = SUM(salary) / COUNT(salary), where COUNT only counts rows where salary IS NOT NULL.

questions.prompt: Which statement calculates revenue from completed orders?

options.label: B
options.text: SELECT SUM(total_amount) FROM orders WHERE status = 'Completed'

options.label: C
options.text: SELECT COUNT(total_amount) FROM orders WHERE status = 'Completed'

options.label: D
options.text: SELECT SUM(total_amount) FROM orders WHERE status = 'Cancelled'

questions.explanation: You must combine WHERE to filter status = 'Completed' BEFORE SUM(total_amount). Without the filter, SUM would add Cancelled / Pending orders too → wrong result.

questions.prompt: Can MIN and MAX be used on date columns?

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, MIN returns the earliest date, MAX returns the latest date

options.label: C
options.text: Yes, but you must cast to a number first

questions.explanation: Yes. MIN(date_col) returns the earliest date, MAX(date_col) returns the latest date. SQL compares dates just like numbers.

questions.prompt: Which function CANNOT be used on a TEXT column?
questions.explanation: PostgreSQL has no SUM(TEXT) or AVG(TEXT): explicitly convert valid numeric text to a suitable type when needed. COUNT, MIN and MAX accept TEXT; string order follows collation rather than a universal alphabet.

lessons.title: Grouping data with GROUP BY
lessons.rawTitle: Bài 27: Grouping data with GROUP BY

theory.contentHtml:
Lesson contents:

  • 1. Why do we need GROUP BY?
  • 2. Basic GROUP BY
  • 3. GROUP BY + multiple functions
  • 4. Grouping by a derived value
  • 5. Which columns can you select after grouping?
  • Important Notes

1. Why do we need GROUP BY?

You want to know the total salary per department. You can't use a simple SUM because it computes over the entire table.

GROUP BY splits the data into groups and applies the aggregate function to each group.

2. Basic GROUP BY

SELECT department, SUM(salary) AS total_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
LIMIT 10;

Result: 4 rows - each row is the total salary of one department.

3. GROUP BY + multiple functions

SELECT department,
       COUNT(*) AS num_emp,
       AVG(salary) AS avg_salary,
       MAX(salary) AS max_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
LIMIT 10;

4. Grouping by a derived value

The column you need to group by is not always there. To see how many orders each month has, the table only holds a full date (2024-01-10), not a "month" column - you have to derive the month and group by that.

GROUP BY can group by an expression, not just an existing column:

SELECT to_char(date_trunc('month', order_date)::date, 'YYYY-MM') AS month,
       COUNT(*) AS num_orders
FROM orders
GROUP BY date_trunc('month', order_date)::date
ORDER BY date_trunc('month', order_date)::date
LIMIT 10;

date_trunc('month', order_date)::date maps every date in a month to its first day. Use to_char(..., 'YYYY-MM') only in the final SELECT for display.

Group and order by the underlying DATE value; the YYYY-MM label is only for display.

PostgreSQL: use date_trunc('month', date_column) for the monthly boundary and to_char(...) only for display formatting. Do not group by a formatted string while date arithmetic is still needed.

5. Which columns can you select after grouping?

A department can have several job titles. When grouping by department, PostgreSQL cannot choose one position to represent the whole department. The following query raises an error, because position is neither grouped nor inside an aggregate function:

SELECT department, position, COUNT(*) AS num_emp
FROM employees
GROUP BY department;

To count employees by department and job title, group by both columns:

SELECT department, position, COUNT(*) AS num_emp
FROM employees
GROUP BY department, position
ORDER BY department, position
LIMIT 10;

Adding position changes the grouping: the result has one row per (department, position) pair, rather than one row per department. If you only need the employee count per department, remove position from SELECT:

SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS num_emp
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
ORDER BY department
LIMIT 10;

Use MIN(position) or MAX(position) only if you actually want the smallest or largest job title according to string comparison order. This does not list every job title in the group.

PostgreSQL exception: if GROUP BY includes the complete declared primary key of a table, you can select other columns of that same table without grouping by them. For example, employees.id is the primary key, so the following query is valid:

SELECT id, full_name, COUNT(*) AS num_rows
FROM employees
GROUP BY id
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 10;

Each id identifies one employee, so each group in this example has one name and num_rows = 1. This is a functional dependency. Values that happen to be unique in the current data do not replace a declared primary key; department is not the primary key of employees either.

See the PostgreSQL GROUP BY rules.

Important Notes

  • In PostgreSQL, columns referenced in SELECT must be grouped, be inside an aggregate function, or meet the primary-key functional dependency exception described above.
  • GROUP BY comes after WHERE (if present)
  • You can GROUP BY multiple columns: GROUP BY department, position

GROUP BY does not sort the result: use ORDER BY for a defined order. Rows with a NULL grouping key belong to the same group. On an empty table, GROUP BY department returns zero groups; an aggregate query without GROUP BY still has one global group.

headings.text: 1. Why do we need GROUP BY?
5. Which columns can you select after grouping?

theory.contentHtml:
Lesson contents:

  • 1. WHERE vs HAVING
  • 2. Basic HAVING
  • 3. Combining WHERE + GROUP BY + HAVING
  • Important Notes

1. WHERE vs HAVING

+--------------------------+----------------------+-----------------------+
|                          |         WHERE        |         HAVING        |
+--------------------------+----------------------+-----------------------+
| Filters                  | Rows before grouping | Groups after GROUP BY |
| Use aggregate functions? | ❌ No                | ✅ Yes                |
+--------------------------+----------------------+-----------------------+

2. Basic HAVING

Keep only departments with more than 3 employees:

SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS num_emp
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3
LIMIT 10;

3. Combining WHERE + GROUP BY + HAVING

SELECT department, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
WHERE position = 'Staff'
GROUP BY department
HAVING AVG(salary) > 15000000
LIMIT 10;
  1. WHERE filters: only staff (not department/team heads)
  2. GROUP BY groups: by department
  3. HAVING filters groups: only departments with average salary > 15 million

Important Notes

  • When these clauses appear together, their written order is: WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING
  • HAVING does not require GROUP BY: without it, the entire input forms one group. A SELECT output alias cannot be used directly in HAVING; repeat the aggregate expression.
  • Remember: WHERE filters rows, HAVING filters groups

A valid PostgreSQL example: return one row only when the table contains employees.

SELECT COUNT(*) AS num_emp
FROM employees
HAVING COUNT(*) > 0;

Lesson contents:

  • 1. The order you write SQL
  • 2. Logical processing order
  • 3. Comprehensive example
  • Important Notes

1. The order you write SQL

SELECT column           -- 1. Choose columns
FROM table_name         -- 2. From which table
WHERE condition         -- 3. Filter rows
GROUP BY group_column   -- 4. Group
HAVING group_condition  -- 5. Filter groups
ORDER BY sort_column    -- 6. Sort
LIMIT n;                -- 7. Limit

2. Logical processing order

This model explains the meaning of a query, not a required physical execution plan. PostgreSQL may choose different access paths and push filters down. Logical processing order:

  1. FROM - Choose table
  2. WHERE - Filter rows
  3. GROUP BY - Group
  4. HAVING - Filter groups
  5. SELECT - Choose columns
  6. ORDER BY - Sort
  7. LIMIT - Limit

That's why you cannot use a SELECT output alias in WHERE:

-- WRONG: SELECT output aliases are not in scope in WHERE
SELECT salary * 12 AS annual_salary
FROM employees
WHERE annual_salary > 300000000
LIMIT 10;

-- ✅ CORRECT: use the original expression
SELECT salary * 12 AS annual_salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary * 12 > 300000000
LIMIT 10;

3. Comprehensive example

"Top 3 departments with the highest total salary, counting only employees who have a salary":

SELECT department,
       COUNT(*) AS num_emp,
       SUM(salary) AS total_salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY department
ORDER BY total_salary DESC, department
LIMIT 3;

Important Notes

  • Remember the order: S-F-W-G-H-O-L (SELECT FROM WHERE GROUP HAVING ORDER LIMIT)
  • PostgreSQL allows SELECT output aliases in ORDER BY and GROUP BY, but not in WHERE or HAVING; table aliases are valid in WHERE.
  • Not every query needs all 7 parts - use only what's necessary

questions.prompt: In PostgreSQL, when grouping employees by department (which is not the primary key), how can you include position in SELECT?

options.label: B
options.text: Add position to GROUP BY or put position inside an aggregate function

questions.explanation: department is not the primary key, and a department can have several position values. PostgreSQL raises an error if you select position directly while grouping only by department. GROUP BY department, position counts each department and job-title pair; MIN(position) or MAX(position) selects just one value according to string comparison order. If you only need the employee count per department, remove position from SELECT. Functional dependency exception: when GROUP BY includes the complete declared primary key, other columns of that same table can be selected without further grouping.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between WHERE and HAVING?

options.label: B
options.text: WHERE filters rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY

options.label: C
options.text: WHERE is for numbers, HAVING is for strings

questions.explanation: WHERE filters ROWS BEFORE GROUP BY (cannot use aggregates). HAVING filters GROUPS AFTER GROUP BY (can use aggregates: HAVING COUNT(*) > 5). This is the core difference. HAVING also works without GROUP BY: the entire input is one group.

questions.prompt: What is the written clause order for the SELECT statement below?

options.label: A
options.text: SELECT → FROM → GROUP BY → WHERE → ORDER BY

options.label: B
options.text: SELECT → FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY → LIMIT

options.label: C
options.text: FROM → SELECT → WHERE → ORDER BY → GROUP BY

options.label: D
options.text: SELECT → WHERE → FROM → ORDER BY → LIMIT

questions.explanation: The answer gives the WRITTEN order: SELECT → FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY → LIMIT. Logical processing starts FROM → WHERE; it is not a required PostgreSQL physical execution plan.

questions.prompt: Why can a SELECT output alias not be referenced directly in WHERE at the same query level?

options.label: B
options.text: SELECT output aliases are outside the name scope searched by WHERE

options.label: C
options.text: Aliases are only used in ORDER BY

options.label: D
options.text: This is only an exception in one database engine

questions.explanation: PostgreSQL permits SELECT output aliases in GROUP BY and ORDER BY, not in WHERE/HAVING at the same level. Repeat the expression or use a subquery/CTE; table aliases such as e.salary are valid in WHERE.
